punchline: Dilbert's guess that they are 'nobody' dinosaurs, so unnoticed that they could hide unseen, is confirmed with a pun on 'nobody' plus '-saurus', which also echoes their names Bob and Dawn.
summary: A pair of surviving dinosaurs reveal they have been lurking in a man's house and cheerfully accept a pun about being unnoticeable.

title: Dilbert Falls for Junk Mail Prize

situation: Dilbert reads a mailer and excitedly explains that he can win a Jeep Cherokee or a valuable mock emerald just by driving two hours and enduring a condo sales pitch. Dogbert, sitting nearby, responds by insulting his intelligence.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically implies that Dilbert is gullible and has a fake brain, so a fake emerald is the only prize he'll ever get.
summary: A man thrilled by a too-good-to-be-true mailer gets mocked by his dog for being foolish enough to believe it.

punchline: Abandoning logic for 'creativity' only made the invention worse, so it still doesn't work and now Dilbert is also miserable.
summary: Told to trade analytical thinking for creativity, an engineer tinkers with his gadget and ends up with a broken device and tears.

summary: A man regrets not exchanging contact details with a dream date he imagined overnight.

summary: Dogbert stalks his owner like a nature-documentary hunter, luring him with pastry and pelting him with a slingshot.

punchline: Dogbert reassures Dilbert about his manliness, then undercuts him by predicting an even more humiliating failure: dying by his own necktie.
summary: After insisting he never doubted his friend's toughness, a small dog suggests the man's real problem would be tragically mistaking his tie for a parachute handle.

punchline: Dogbert's example of a safe, general prediction is the one thing guaranteed to come true, exposing fortune-telling as vague and unfalsifiable.
summary: A trainee swami dog shows his skeptical client how fortune tellers stay safe by predicting something nobody can dispute.

title: Rocks Are Silly Money

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on a rock wall overlooking green hills and discuss the world economy. punchline: If you're going to base money on rocks, you should at least pick a common one, which pokes fun at the arbitrary scarcity behind gold's value.
summary: Two friends on a hillside mock humanity's gold-based economy as primitive rock-trading, then suggest it would be smarter to use rocks that are easy to find.

situation: Dilbert is relaxing in an armchair reading a book while Dogbert asks why he bothers. Dilbert is alarmed and Dogbert blames the librarians for hiding the danger.
punchline: Dogbert strings together familiar sayings (knowledge is power, power corrupts, crime doesn't pay) into a absurd syllogism that reading causes poverty, then pins the cover-up on librarians.
summary: Dogbert twists a chain of well-known proverbs into a ridiculous argument that reading will bankrupt his owner.

summary: Dogbert unveils an absurd clothing gadget and, once it seems plausible, immediately upsells a companion product that makes it actually usable.

punchline: Dilbert gets excited over a subscription that mails him one piece of toast, showing how lonely and starved of excitement his life is.
summary: A man eagerly fetches his mail only to find a lone slice of bread-based treat, which delights him far more than it should.

punchline: Dogbert, who wanted to rule the world, settles for a live elf as a minion, and Dilbert mistakes the captive elf for a G.I. Joe doll, unwittingly hinting at Dogbert's dominating nature.
summary: A would-be world dictator dog scales down his Christmas wish to a single elf servant, which his owner mistakes for an action figure.

summary: A dinner date meant to show off his worldliness ends with Dilbert shredding the restaurant's linen by mistake, which his dog finds unremarkable.

transcript.text: You know what I hate?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate it when hundreds of people get together and throw a surprise birthday party for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's amazing how nature protects us from the things we hate.

setting: Outdoors on a rocky hilltop under a blue sky
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on rocks outdoors. Dilbert says he hates it when hundreds of people throw him a surprise birthday party. Dogbert replies that nature protects us from the things we hate.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically implies that nobody would ever throw Dilbert a party, since the thing he claims to hate is something that will never happen because nobody cares enough about him.
summary: Dogbert wryly notes that the universe conveniently shields Dilbert from a party he dreads because no one would ever organize it.

title: Dogbert's Affirmation: Dilbert Eaten by Slug

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's all the writing for?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's called "affirmations."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The theory is that if you write down your objective fifteen times a day, the objective will be achieved, no matter how unlikely.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you've written "Dilbert will be eaten by a garden slug."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's all I could think of.

setting: Dilbert's desk or office
situation: Dogbert sits at a desk repeatedly writing on a sheet of paper. When Dilbert asks what it's for, Dogbert explains the self-help technique of affirmations, where writing a goal repeatedly supposedly makes it come true. Dilbert reads the paper and discovers the goal is for him to be eaten by a garden slug.
punchline: Dogbert's chosen objective is the absurdly unlikely death of Dilbert by garden slug, and he admits it was simply the best he could come up with, implying he's using the technique mockingly or out of spite.
summary: A dog scribbles a self-help ritual over and over, and his human discovers the wished-for outcome is his own bizarre demise.

title: Dogbert Mishears Can of Balls

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.text: I'll be right back.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sorry. Turns out we don't need you after all.

setting: A tennis court
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, his tennis partner, whether he brought a can of balls. Dogbert mishears this as 'cannibals' and leaves to fetch one. He returns and dismisses the cannibal he has brought, who then offers to eat the loser of the match instead.
punchline: Dogbert misheard 'can of balls' as 'cannibals' and brought a real cannibal to the tennis match, who now wants to eat whoever loses.
summary: A tennis game goes awry when a misheard request leads to a hungry tribesman showing up on court.

title: Dogbert's Skydiving Sound Effects

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thud...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean "thud...ouch!" or just "thud"?

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert, relaxing in an armchair, asks Dogbert for a single good reason not to take skydiving lessons. Dogbert answers only with the sound of a body hitting the ground. Dilbert calmly asks whether that thud would be painful or instantly fatal.
punchline: Dogbert's one-word answer implies the parachute fails and Dilbert dies on impact, and Dilbert responds with deadpan curiosity about whether he would feel any pain first.
summary: Asked to talk his friend out of a risky hobby, a dog simply imitates the sound of a fatal landing, and the friend wonders how much it would hurt.

punchline: The possessed furniture identifies itself as an 'Upholsterygeist', a pun combining upholstery and poltergeist.
summary: A dog calls his owner at work to say the household furniture is haunted, and the ghostly armchair introduces itself with an upholstery-flavoured pun.

situation: Dogbert stands on a stool at the bathroom sink and asks whether he resembles famous movie and TV dogs. Dilbert, standing half-dressed by the shower, says he looks like a big furry egg. Dogbert, sitting on a stool, then declares he feels inspired and ready to face the day.
punchline: Dogbert treats a blunt insult as a motivational pep talk, with the sarcasm implying he is either oblivious or gets his confidence from anywhere.
summary: A dog hoping to be compared to famous canine stars gets likened to an egg and cheerfully takes it as encouragement.

transcript.text: Don't get too far from salt.

setting: Office desk
situation: Dogbert sits at a desk repeatedly writing on paper as an experiment with affirmations, apparently writing that Dilbert will be eaten by a garden slug. Dilbert wonders whether it could work, then talks himself out of it with logic. Dogbert replies with a warning to stay close to salt.
punchline: Dogbert's sly warning about salt, which kills slugs, shows he is happily hedging that the affirmation might work, undercutting Dilbert's confidence in logic.
summary: A dog scribbles a bizarre prophecy about his coworker's fate, and the coworker's rational dismissal is met with a quietly ominous tip.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, sitting near a desk
situation: Dogbert announces he will dedicate his life to helping the less fortunate. Dilbert praises the idea and guesses he'll help the homeless or hungry. Dogbert reveals his actual target group is people who failed to buy real estate in the 1970s.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of the 'less fortunate' is people who missed out on a real estate boom, a trivial misfortune compared to homelessness or hunger, with charity as an afterthought.
summary: The self-serving dog pledges to help the unlucky, but the first group on his list turns out to be those who skipped the housing market decades ago.

situation: Dilbert walks into an electronics store and calmly asks the clerk for a detonator coil suitable for a small nuclear device. The clerk faints and collapses to the floor with a thump. Dilbert then remarks that this was the best reaction he has gotten all day.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately goes around shocking store clerks with outrageous requests and rates their fainting reactions like a game or hobby.
summary: A man strolls into an electronics shop with an alarming request, then gleefully scores the clerk's swooning collapse against his other pranks that day.

situation: Dilbert reads a newspaper at the table and asks Dogbert for his opinion on the Soviet policy of openness. Dogbert, sitting across from him with a cup of coffee, claims he isn't sure Gorbachev even exists, then explains he is simply 'glasnostic'. Dilbert reacts by saying he shouldn't let Dogbert drink coffee.
punchline: Dogbert turns 'glasnost' into a pun on 'agnostic' to claim doubt about Gorbachev's existence, and Dilbert groans at the wordplay by blaming the coffee.
summary: Asked about Soviet openness, a doubtful dog coins a terrible pun and gets cut off from caffeine.

title: Dogbert Mocks Einstein Time Logic

transcript.text: According to Einstein, time slows down as you approach the speed of light.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Didn't he also prove that time flies when you're having fun?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Were we finished here?

setting: Outdoors, on rocks under a blue sky
situation: Dilbert sits on a rock and explains a piece of Einstein's physics to Dogbert. Dogbert responds by mashing it together with the saying that time flies when you're having fun, building a nonsensical conclusion. He then asks whether Dilbert is done talking.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately confuses scientific theory with a folksy proverb to show how silly the logic gets, then dismisses Dilbert's lecture as a waste of time.
summary: A casual physics lecture gets derailed when a dog fuses relativity with a cliché and then asks to leave.

setting: A prehistoric-themed scene, apparently a presentation or lecture, with Dilbert sitting in a chair listening
situation: A green dinosaur tells Dilbert a tale about Larry the dinosaur, who survived a meteor strike that wiped out the others. Dilbert, seated next to a gray horned creature, rejects the story.
punchline: The invented evolutionary species, the "Doctor-Billed Flattypuss," is a pun on platypus and a doctor's bill, depicted as a dollar bill walking upright, and Dilbert refuses to accept the groan-worthy pun.
summary: A dinosaur spins a silly tale in which a meteor survivor's huge hospital bills spawn a new species that is half platypus, half money, and Dilbert isn't convinced.

title: Dilbert's Plant Leaves a Note

transcript.text: What's this little piece of paper?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert kneels beside a broken flowerpot with a spilled plant on the floor and explains that he was talking to the plant as usual when it fell off his desk. Dogbert investigates, finds a little piece of paper among the wreckage, and reads it aloud as a note from the plant.
punchline: The plant apparently left a suicide note, implying that Dilbert's constant talking drove it to jump off the desk.
summary: A houseplant takes a fatal tumble from a desk, and the note beside it suggests its owner's chatter was the cause.

Dogbert is clearly carrying a stack of rolled documents or plans.
punchline: Dogbert's cold-blooded betrayal of Dilbert is waved away with the glib claim that the target is the Soviet 'Evil Empire', as if that justified selling out his master.
summary: A sinister spy bargains with Dogbert for Dilbert's confidential data, and Dogbert later brushes off Dilbert's alarm by invoking Cold War rhetoric.

situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert his new invention, which he calls the "Dick Tracy" watch. Dogbert responds by describing a watch that transmits voices and pictures and would revolutionize life. Dilbert says that sounds much harder than what he actually planned.
punchline: Dilbert's invention is just a watch with a picture of Dick Tracy glued on it, a trivial idea that falls far short of the futuristic communication device Dogbert imagines.
summary: A man proudly unveils a gadget named after a comic-strip detective, only to realize his dog's visionary interpretation is far more ambitious than his own simple novelty.

situation: Dilbert muses to Dogbert that people walk differently when they know they are being watched. Dogbert flatly says he has never noticed. Dogbert then asks if Dilbert needs to go anywhere, and Dilbert replies with a taunt about Dogbert's legs, inviting him to go first.
punchline: Dilbert's remark about self-conscious walking turns into a jab at Dogbert, implying Dogbert is the one who walks oddly and is embarrassed to be watched.
summary: A casual observation about how people stride when observed turns into a petty standoff over who has to walk away first.

punchline: Dogbert assumes the uncle will ignore Dilbert's offenses out of family loyalty, but Dilbert deadpans that the favoritism is bought with bribes.
summary: A pun about legal-sized paper gives way to a deadpan admission that Dilbert keeps his police relative friendly by mailing him bribes.

Dogbert says he assumed there would be no tombstone, and Dilbert guesses he would be cremated. Dogbert coolly adds that he might have Dilbert stuffed instead, depending on cost.
punchline: Dogbert treats his friend's death purely as a budgeting decision, suggesting taxidermy if it saves money.
summary: A man asks his dog about his own memorial and learns the pet plans to dispose of his remains in whichever way costs least.

summary: A cocky angler is dragged into the lake by his catch, much to his companion's amusement.

punchline: Dogbert's made-up answer plays on golfers' stereotypes of loud plaid clothing and fibbing about their scores, so Dilbert realizes he is being fed nonsense instead of real science.
summary: Dogbert backs up a supposed scientific discovery with jokes about golfers' clothes and dishonesty, leaving Dilbert doubting him as a news source.

summary: A nervous driver fusses over a routine toll payment and then muses about his odd need to be liked by the person in the booth.

summary: A man rambling about a long-ago meal answers his friend's mocking request for exact dates with earnest, dull speculation.

summary: Dogbert lectures a silent, newspaper-reading Dilbert on how misplaced eyes would doom mankind through a chain of far-fetched consequences.

summary: A brainy talking dog learns how ordinary dogs behave and wryly decides they would make poor board-game partners.

punchline: Dilbert thinks tracking a woman's movements with software to stage a fake coincidence is more natural than just asking her out, which is absurd and slightly creepy.

punchline: Dilbert's dream of winning the sweepstakes is crushed by his own trivial mistake, as the famous prize patrol visitor is only there to return his unstamped entry.
summary: A celebrity prize-announcer shows up at a man's door, but instead of a jackpot he brings back the entry that never got mailed.

title: Dilbert's Snoring Sounds Like Whales

transcript.speaker: Tape recorder
transcript.text: Eoowaha geowmzla

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table with a tape player
situation: Dogbert plays Dilbert a recording of loud snoring that he claims he made the night before. Dilbert denies snoring and points out that the tape box is labeled as National Geographic's whale songs. Dogbert turns this around, saying that means even National Geographic can't tell Dilbert's snoring from a whale.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to discredit the recording backfires because Dogbert twists it into an admission that his snoring is indistinguishable from a giant whale.
summary: A man disputes a tape of his snoring by citing the box's whale-song label, only to have his dog turn the point into an insult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: A grocery store, near the produce aisle and checkout
situation: Dilbert is pushing a cart through the grocery store when a clerk stops him, having seen him eat a grape. Dilbert assumes he is being accused of shoplifting, but the clerk says he only wants to make sure Dilbert pays for it. The clerk then weighs Dilbert on the checkout scale to charge him for the grape.
punchline: The clerk charges by weight, so he weighs Dilbert before and after, and Dilbert replies that he was "Happy" before he came in, a sour joke about how being weighed and charged for a grape ruins his mood.
summary: A store clerk takes the idea of paying for a sampled grape to absurd lengths by weighing the customer on the checkout scale.

title: Dilbert's Starving Ego Leaves Home

situation: Dilbert is startled by a small, lumpy creature that announces itself as his ego. When he asks why it is outside his body, the ego explains that Dilbert has been starving it of nourishment. It says it is leaving to audition for a play, presumably to get the attention it needs.
punchline: Dilbert's ego is so underfed from his lack of self-esteem that it has physically left him to seek validation by acting in a play.
summary: A tiny, malnourished embodiment of Dilbert's ego walks out on him because he never gives it the attention it craves.

setting: Outdoors or an office-area walkway, with a plain light blue background
situation: Dilbert tells the Grim Reaper he has the wrong person and asks to be left alone. Death says he doesn't want to waste a trip in case Dilbert's number comes up tomorrow, and asks to simply hang around for the day. Dilbert walks on with Death trailing right behind him, and Death asks how he feels.
punchline: Death promises to be unnoticeable but immediately becomes an annoying, hovering presence, repeatedly checking on Dilbert's health like a morbidly eager hanger-on.
summary: A reaper who has made a mistake refuses to go home empty-handed and shadows a weary office worker, hopefully inquiring about his well-being.

situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit on rocks outdoors while Dilbert asks Dogbert what he would do if he had everything he wanted. Dogbert says he would gloat, make others feel like failures and live a garish, decadent life. When Dilbert asks what he would do once that gets boring, Dogbert says he might start a perfume company.
punchline: Dogbert's idea of the ultimate ambition after a life of smug excess is to launch a celebrity-style perfume line, poking fun at the way rich people eventually brand themselves into fragrances.
summary: Asked what he would do with unlimited wishes, Dogbert outlines a life of smug excess and then settles on selling scent as his fallback hobby.

title: Dogbert's Self-Confidence Seminar Scam

situation: Dilbert holds a newspaper containing an ad for Doctor Dogbert's self-confidence seminar and asks his dog what the scam is. Dogbert candidly explains that he plans to gather meek, easily led people to do his bidding, then leverage that power into wealth or world domination. Dilbert responds by scolding him as if he were a misbehaving pet.
punchline: Dogbert lays out a megalomaniacal plan to conquer the world, and Dilbert's only reaction is to scold him like a badly behaved house pet.
summary: A scheming dog reveals his plan to turn a confidence-building seminar into a path to world domination, and his owner merely chides him for it.

A loud noise follows, and Dogbert coolly explains the Johnsons weren't home.
punchline: Dogbert casually sends the demolition crew to destroy his neighbors' house, and the loud crash is passed off as nothing more than the Johnsons being out.
summary: A demolition worker with the wrong address is cheerfully steered by a dog toward the neighbors' house, which promptly gets flattened.

punchline: Contrary to the old saying, Dan Quayle clearly does not put his pants on one leg at a time, and his exasperated wife thinks this is a recurring embarrassment, mocking his reputation for being foolish.
summary: A reassuring cliché about a famous politician's ordinary habits is undercut by a glimpse of him hopelessly entangled in his own trousers.

summary: A new manager asks to be addressed by his first name, and an employee mistakes the request for a command to get down on the floor.

title: Awkward Synchronized Hallway Walking Dilemma

punchline: Dilbert's absurd escape from a trivial social awkwardness, sneaking into the ladies' room, is sarcastically praised by Dogbert as preserving his dignity.
summary: A man so dreads awkwardly mirroring a stranger's steps in a hallway that he resorts to a ridiculous ruse to escape, earning a dry compliment from his dog.

setting: An office hallway, then Dilbert's home

He asks himself what etiquette demands for a third encounter. He then tells Dogbert that he solved it by pulling the fire alarm.
punchline: Dilbert's social anxiety is so extreme that causing a building-wide evacuation seems a reasonable way to avoid an awkward third hallway greeting.
summary: A man too uncomfortable to face a repeat hallway encounter with an acquaintance resorts to setting off the fire alarm.

title: Dating Myself Over Ice Cream

situation: Dilbert sits on a hillside eating an ice cream cone and reminisces about when cones cost only fifteen cents. He remarks that this reveals his age, saying he's 'dating himself.' Dogbert, sitting beside him, replies that nobody else would date him anyway.
punchline: Dogbert takes the idiom 'dating myself' literally and insults Dilbert by implying he is so undateable that dating himself is his only option.
summary: While reminiscing about old prices, a man jokes about revealing his age and his dog deadpans that he has no romantic prospects.

While out walking, Dogbert loudly calls out to passersby, advertising Dilbert as a single male. Dilbert, embarrassed, says the method is overrated while Dogbert tells an imagined crowd to queue up.
punchline: Dogbert's crude catcalling and mock crowd control turn Dilbert's dating plan into a humiliating spectacle, with the sarcastic implication that droves of women will line up.
summary: A dating tip from a book goes awry when the dog takes over the pursuit and shouts for attention on his owner's behalf.

punchline: Hell's eternal damnation is being justified by a trivial fast-food ketchup infraction, and the devil's punishment is merely mocking shame.
summary: A devil with a giant spoon condemns a newly arrived Dilbert over a stolen ketchup packet.

summary: A man tidying his yard is confronted by an indignant Mother Nature who takes his raking as criticism of her housekeeping and punishes him like a scolded child.

summary: A man privately confesses he has been faking adulthood since his teens and assumes women are different, until a coworker's thought bubble proves otherwise.

title: The Reusable Generic Newspaper Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Look! I've created the world's first completely reusable newspaper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pope denounces violence... Home prices rise... Unrest in the Mideast...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Generic news!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A thousand bucks. You'll never need another one.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, a plain room
situation: Dogbert shows Dilbert a newspaper he claims is the first completely reusable one. Dilbert reads the headlines, which are vague stories that are always true, and Dogbert calls it generic news. Dilbert asks the price and Dogbert pitches it at a thousand dollars.
punchline: The headlines are so perennially repeated that one newspaper could serve forever, and Dogbert exploits this to sell an absurdly overpriced product.
summary: Dogbert peddles an expensive newspaper filled with timeless headlines that never go out of date.

title: Underpaid Criminals Aren't Really Bad

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's an interesting editorial...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This guy says we should increase the pay of congressmen to remove incentive for them to engage in illegal acts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: By that theory, criminals aren't bad, just underpaid.

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair reading a newspaper while Dogbert rests on his outstretched legs. Dilbert reads aloud an editorial arguing that raising congressmen's pay would remove their incentive to commit illegal acts. Dogbert responds by applying the same logic to criminals in general.
punchline: Dogbert points out that the editorial's logic would excuse all crime as merely a matter of insufficient pay, exposing how absurd it is to treat corruption as a salary problem.
summary: A newspaper proposal to pay politicians more so they will stop breaking the law gets a dry rebuttal from the dog on his owner's lap.

title: Bear Skin Rug Kit Refund Scam

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ding dong

transcript.speaker: Bear
transcript.text: Hi. I'm the bear skin rug you ordered by mail.

transcript.speaker: Bear
transcript.text: I'm a kit. You just have to kill me, rip my guts out and leave me to dry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Egad! I couldn't possibly do that. Please... just go.

transcript.speaker: Bear
transcript.text: You'll receive a full refund, of course.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, no! Please keep it.

transcript.speaker: Man at desk
transcript.text: How were sales today?

transcript.speaker: Bear
transcript.text: Great! Sold myself seven times.

setting: Dilbert's home workbench and doorway, then a Bear Rugs sales office
situation: Dilbert answers his door and finds a live bear claiming to be the bear skin rug kit he ordered by mail, requiring him to kill and gut it himself. Horrified, Dilbert refuses, and the bear offers a refund, which Dilbert waves off so the bear can keep the money. Back at the Bear Rugs office, the bear proudly reports to his boss that he has sold himself seven times.
punchline: The bear has a scam going where customers are too squeamish to follow through, so he collects the payment and keeps reselling himself.
summary: A live bear delivers himself as a do-it-yourself rug kit, and when buyers recoil he simply moves on and resells himself again and again.

title: Frozen Cavemen Date Excuse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Helen just canceled our date.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What excuse this time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently she discovered tiny frozen cavemen in her ice cube trays and she's trying to revive them for science.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you the least bit suspicious of that story?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah... How do I know they aren't just actors pretending to be cavemen?

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that his girlfriend Helen has canceled their date, claiming she found tiny frozen cavemen in her ice cube trays and is reviving them for science. Dogbert asks if he is suspicious of the story. Dilbert says he is, but his doubt is only that the cavemen might be actors.
punchline: Dilbert is skeptical of the absurd excuse, but only about the wrong detail, doubting whether the tiny cavemen are real cavemen rather than doubting that tiny frozen cavemen could exist at all.
summary: A man's girlfriend blows him off with a ridiculous excuse, and his skepticism fixates on the one detail that misses the real absurdity.

title: Dilbert Insults a Drinking Fountain

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate this... When I'm really thirsty, there always seems to be some disgusting public fountain to taunt me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No doubt this thing is crawling with cooties. And I'll have to wrap my lips around it to slurp the water out.

transcript.speaker: Water Fountain
transcript.text: Hey, I'm not too thrilled about you, either.

setting: Office hallway beside a public drinking fountain
situation: Dilbert, very thirsty, stands over a public drinking fountain and complains that it must be covered in germs and that he will have to put his mouth on it. In the last panel the fountain talks back and says it isn't happy about him either.
punchline: Dilbert is so busy being disgusted by the fountain that he never considers the fountain might find having his mouth on it just as unpleasant.
summary: A thirsty man grumbles about the germs on a public fountain until the fountain snaps back with its own complaint.

title: Practicing Laughter in the Bedroom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hoo-hoo-hee-ha! ...No, that's not it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you suppose other people practice laughing when they're alone?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Time for your sneezing drill.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Other people make it look so natural.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom
situation: Dilbert stands at his dresser mirror rehearsing a laugh and decides it sounds wrong. He asks Dogbert whether other people practice laughing alone, and Dogbert assures him they do, then announces it's time for his sneezing drill. Dilbert sits on the bed and laments how natural others make these things look.
punchline: Dilbert's social awkwardness is so extreme that he must rehearse basic involuntary reactions like laughing and sneezing, and Dogbert's matter-of-fact coaching confirms how unnatural he is.
summary: A painfully awkward engineer rehearses his laugh in the mirror and then his dog schedules practice for sneezing too.

title: Dogbert Hates Heavy Metal, Meaning Opera

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You know what kind of music I hate?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When they wear those outrageous outfits, scream like tortured weasels and nobody understands the words.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heavy metal rock?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Opera.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair and Dogbert on the footrest
situation: Dogbert lounges on the footrest in front of Dilbert's armchair and asks if Dilbert knows what music he hates. He describes performers in outrageous outfits screaming like tortured weasels while nobody can understand the words. Dilbert guesses heavy metal rock, but Dogbert says he means opera.
punchline: The description sounds exactly like heavy metal, but Dogbert is actually describing opera, poking fun at its screeching vocals and incomprehensible lyrics.
summary: A dog's rant about a hated music genre leads his owner to guess the wrong one, with the surprise answer being opera.

title: Dilbert's Program Generates Pick-Up Line

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've designed this program to generate the most effective pick-up line in the universe.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! Women will be helpless when they hear my clever opener.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and the line is...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Hi. I'm Mel Gibson. Did you see a dingo dog go by here with my shirt?"

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Kiss me, you wicked savage.

setting: Dilbert's office desk with his computer
situation: Dilbert boasts to Dogbert that he has written a program to generate the most effective pick-up line ever. After building suspense, he reads out the line: a self-introduction as Mel Gibson asking about a dingo dog with his shirt. Dogbert responds with a seductive reply, apparently falling for it.
punchline: The pick-up line is so absurd it only works on a dog, since a dingo dog is the one audience that would be charmed, so Dilbert's 'most effective line' only impresses Dogbert.
summary: A programmer's proudly engineered seduction line turns out to be a silly joke that only his pet dog finds irresistible.

title: Soup, Necktie, and Gravity Experiment

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't quite understand what scientific principle you intend to discover with a bowl of soup and a necktie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm testing the strange attraction between staining liquids and new ties.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wonder how Newton missed this little gravitational oddity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He didn't wear a necktie.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Foosh!

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table with a bowl of soup
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert what scientific principle he hopes to discover with a bowl of soup and a necktie. Dilbert explains he is testing the attraction between staining liquids and new ties, then flings the tie at the bowl and gets soup splashed all over himself. Dogbert quips that Newton missed the oddity, and Dilbert replies that Newton never wore a necktie.
punchline: Dilbert's deliberate experiment is really just him ruining his own tie and shirt, and his reply to Dogbert's Newton jab shows he is cleverly justifying a messy, self-inflicted accident as science.
summary: Dilbert stages a silly science experiment that ends with soup splattered across his chest, and he shrugs it off with a witty answer about history's greatest physicist.

title: Monkeys Could Write Better Poetry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well? What do you think of my new poem?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I once read that given infinite time, a thousand monkeys with typewriters would eventually write the entire works of Shakespeare.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But what about my poem?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Three monkeys, ten minutes.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a table
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for his opinion of a new poem he has written. Dogbert, holding the pages, answers with the infinite monkey theorem about monkeys eventually writing Shakespeare. When Dilbert presses him about his own poem, Dogbert says three monkeys could write it in ten minutes.
punchline: Dogbert insults the poem by saying it is so bad that just three monkeys could produce it in only ten minutes, far less than the infinite time needed for Shakespeare.
summary: Dogbert dismisses Dilbert's amateur verse by claiming a few monkeys with typewriters could crank it out in minutes.

title: Babbling Technical Jargon Until Everyone Sleeps

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: Well, Dilbert, will our idea work from a technical perspective?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wasn't listening... Now I'll have to babble about irrelevant technical things until they lose consciousness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And in conclusion, never underestimate the power of technology.

setting: Conference room during a meeting
situation: At a meeting, a colleague asks Dilbert whether the team's idea will work technically, but Dilbert wasn't paying attention. He decides to bore everyone with irrelevant technical talk until they pass out. By the final panel the attendees are slumped asleep and Dilbert wraps up with a bland conclusion.
punchline: Dilbert uses dull, irrelevant technical jargon as a weapon, putting the whole meeting to sleep so nobody notices he never had an answer.
summary: Caught not listening, an engineer avoids answering a question by lulling the entire meeting into slumber with technobabble.

title: Police Artist Sketches the Victim

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was mugged, but I got a good look at him.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: I'll get a police artist.

transcript.speaker: Police Artist
transcript.text: ...a big head, and kind of a frightened expression...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perfect. Looks just like me. Now let's do the mugger. He was sort of off to the left here.

setting: A police station
situation: Dilbert reports being mugged at a police station and says he got a good look at the attacker. A police artist begins drawing from his description, but the sketch ends up showing a big head and a frightened expression. Dilbert realizes the drawing is of himself and asks to start on the mugger.
punchline: Dilbert's description of the mugger was so dominated by his own fear and perspective that the sketch turned out to be a portrait of himself, the victim.
summary: A mugging victim's sketch artist produces a perfect likeness of the victim rather than the attacker.

title: Dogbert Glues Suction Cups on Kitten

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, I'd like to have a word with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The neighbor says you glued little suction cups on their new kitten and stuck him on their windshield.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's the problem, some kind of copyright infringement?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your second guess?

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert confronts Dogbert, who is relaxing on a pillow next to a radio playing music. He says the neighbor reported that Dogbert glued suction cups onto their new kitten and stuck it on a car windshield. Dogbert responds by guessing the problem is copyright infringement, and Dilbert sarcastically asks for a second guess.
punchline: Dogbert, having done something obviously cruel, can only think the objection is a legal technicality like copyright infringement, ignoring the plain animal cruelty, which Dilbert points out by asking for a second guess.
summary: Dilbert scolds his dog for turning a neighbor's kitten into a windshield ornament, and the dog cluelessly wonders if it's an intellectual property issue.

title: Three Pens Is Bold Fashion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Notice anything different, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing three pens, not just two.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a pretty bold fashion statement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I was out of control.

setting: Plain room, likely Dilbert's home or office, with Dogbert sitting on a small couch
situation: Dilbert proudly asks Dogbert if he notices anything different about him. After an awkward pause, Dilbert reveals he is wearing three pens in his shirt pocket instead of his usual two. Dogbert sarcastically calls it a bold fashion statement, and Dilbert earnestly agrees that he went wild.
punchline: Dilbert considers adding a single extra pen to his pocket a daring, reckless act, showing how dull and risk-averse his idea of rebellion is.
summary: A painfully cautious engineer shows off his one tiny wardrobe change and brags about how wild he has become.

title: Studying Mail Carriers Like Wildlife

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! The post office is complaining that you attacked a mail carrier.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell them that I love mail carriers and would never try to hurt one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently they object to the tranquilizer darts and homing transmitters.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But how else can we learn their migration patterns?

setting: Dilbert's home, by the telephone
situation: Dilbert answers a phone call from the post office, which is complaining that Dogbert attacked a mail carrier. Dogbert insists he loves mail carriers and would never hurt one. Dilbert relays that the post office objects to the tranquilizer darts and homing transmitters, and Dogbert defends them as a way to study the carriers' migration patterns.
punchline: Dogbert treats mail carriers like wild animals to be tagged and tracked, and sincerely believes that excuses the darts and transmitters.
summary: Dogbert defends shooting and tagging a postal worker as legitimate scientific research into how mail carriers roam.
